component.name: BifroSSH
component.summary: GUI SSH client with built-in SFTP and keychain management

description.p: BifroSSH is a modern SSH client with a full terminal emulator, SFTP file browser, SSH key management, per-server theming, and codeprints for quick command access.

ul.li: SFTP file browser with upload, download, and folder navigation
SSH key management with encrypted local keychain
Customisable themes including a built-in theme editor
Codeprints: named commands that can be pasted or run in any session

description.p: The key that encrypts your saved passwords and private keys no longer has to sit in a file beside them. On first launch you choose where it is kept: in your desktop keyring with a passphrase to fall back on, or behind a passphrase alone, or in a file as before. All three remain reachable from Settings, which now reports where the key actually is rather than the best place it could be.

Where a passphrase is used, one can be generated for you as eight words. Capitalisation and spacing are ignored when it is typed back, because it is written on paper and read back later, and that is when transcription goes wrong.

The whole of the stored data is encrypted now, not only the credentials, so hostnames, usernames, jump host chains, forwarding rules and saved commands are no longer readable in the file. That file is also written so an interrupted save cannot destroy it, is readable only by your own account, and keeps the previous version alongside it to recover from.
The window is served a Content Security Policy, and the application identifier now matches the one everything else already used.

Packaging only, with no changes to the application itself. Releases are now built, signed and published from a clean checkout rather than from a developer machine, so what is published is reproducible from the tagged source alone.

A server that is not reachable directly can now be reached through a bastion, the same as ssh's ProxyJump. Pick any other saved host as a host's jump host, and chains of them are followed one link at a time.

Every hop is a full connection of its own: it uses its own stored credentials, and its host key is checked and confirmed separately, so a bastion has to be trusted before it can carry anything. Terminal sessions, file transfers and port forwarding all travel the chain.
Hosts that name a jump host in ~/.ssh/config are now linked up on import instead of being flagged as unsupported.

Whole folders can now be transferred over SFTP, in either direction or between two remote servers, instead of only one file at a time. Progress shows which file of how many is moving, and symbolic links are skipped rather than followed.

Existing hosts can be imported from ~/.ssh/config. The dialog lists what was found before anything is created, skips hosts already saved, and references identity files where they are rather than copying private keys.

Sessions and tunnels now send a keepalive, so they survive NAT and firewall idle timers and report a dead host instead of hanging. Each connection also keeps a log of how it was established, reviewable from the session sidebar after the fact.

Port forwarding rules, codeprints and custom themes are now kept with the rest of your data instead of in browser storage, where clearing browsing data destroyed them. Existing entries are migrated automatically on first launch.
Identities can now authenticate using keys held by a running ssh-agent instead of importing the private key into BifroSSH. The agent signs the challenge, so the key never enters the app.

This covers keys already loaded with ssh-add or held by a desktop keyring, and PIV smartcards and YubiKeys in PIV mode, whose keys cannot be exported and so could not be used at all before. Pick a specific key by fingerprint, or let BifroSSH try each key the agent offers. FIDO security keys are not supported yet, but are ignored rather than preventing the other keys in the agent from working.

BifroSSH can now log in to servers that ask challenge questions instead of accepting a stored credential. That covers PAM setups with password authentication turned off, and two-factor providers such as Duo, TOTP authenticator apps and hardware tokens, none of which could be connected to before.

Set an identity's auth mode to Prompt and nothing is stored for it; the server asks and you answer at connect time. Where the server offers a choice of second factors, the options appear as buttons, so approving a push notification takes a single click. Password and key logins fall back to this automatically.

BifroSSH now verifies the host key of every server it connects to, the same way OpenSSH does. The first time you connect to a server you are shown its fingerprint and asked to confirm it; after that the key is remembered and checked on every connection. If a server ever presents a different key, the connection is refused.

Servers already listed in your ~/.ssh/known_hosts are trusted automatically and will not prompt. A new Known Hosts panel lets you review stored fingerprints, choose how unknown servers are handled, and forget individual hosts.
